newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: COURT TOLD ACCUSED INTENDED FOR BOY TO DIE
The Crown Prosecutor in the case against the man charged over setting fire to a Cairns school boy, has told the court the accused, Paul Wade Streeton, intended to kill Tjandamurra O'Shane.
In the Cairns Supreme Court, 27-year-old Streeton has pleaded not guilty to attempted murder,but guilty to grievous bodily harm with intent to do grievous bodily harm.
Prosecutor John Bailey told court that on October the 10th last year, during big lunch, Tjandamurra was playing tiggy in the school yard of the Cairns North Primary School.
The court heard that at one pm, Streeton poured petrol from a five litre container over Tjandmurra and produced a cigarette lighter.
Mr Bailey said the issue for the jury was one of intent.
WOODS DELAYS LEAVING FOR EUTHANASIA BILL
New South Wales Liberal Senator Bob Woods says he may not leave the Senate for at least another fortnight, despite initially intending to quit politics at the beginning of this month.
Senator Woods, who's under investigation over alleged misuse of Parliamentary expenses, announced last month he would leave the Senate on the March 1 to spend more time with his family.
However the former Coalition front-bencher continues to sit in the Senate, and says he could be there for some time yet.

Senator Woods says while the Opposition has agreed not to take advantage of the Government's reduced numbers should he leave, he's facing a dilemma over the impending vote on the anti-euthanasia Bill.

He says he intends supporting the private members Bill when it comes before the Senate later this month but is having trouble finding somebody opposed to the measure who'll agree not to take part in the vote should he go before it takes place.
CRIME CONFERENCE TOLD TO TARGET CHILDREN
An Australian Institute of Criminology conference in Canberra has been told the prevention of domestic violence needs to start with children.
The institute's Jane Mugford says anti-violence intervention can be done at school and in the home.
She says parents need to be targeted and helped to treat their children differently.
The findings of a comprehensive survey of women who have suffered violence was also presented to the conference.
It shows all women need to be helped in the same way, some only require specific medical or legal help while others need a full crisis refuge.
INDUSTRY BODY SAYS 40,000 JOBS WILL BE LOST OVER TARIFFS
A peak industry body says some 40,000 jobs will be lost in the clothing, textile and footwear industries, unless a target of zero tariffs by 2010, is abandoned.
Tariffs are set to be reduced by half by the Year 2000, with bi-partisan support for a zero tariff regime within another 10-years.
An Australian Chamber of Manufacturers survey has found that only one in eight companies which responded, are sure of surviving in business, if tariffs are removed altogether.
ACM chief executive, Alan Handberg, says the body is asking for a halt to zero reduction for ten years, to give the industry a breather.
REQUEST FOR JOINED CASE AGAINST SEVEN REJECTED
The New South Wales Industrial Commission has rejected an application for Jana Wendt's termination of contract case against Channel Seven to be joined with another.
A senior reporter on the Witness programme, Graeme Davis, asked the commission this morning to wrap his case together with Ms Wendt's, arguing extensive similarities in the two matters.
But Seven opposed the application, claiming in fact there were very few similarities, and that much of the material in each case would be irrelevant in the other.
Justice Frank Marks agreed, and said that although he was mindful of the cost of hearing two separate cases, Ms Wendt's and Mr Davis' contracts were different, and should not be brought together.
NO NEED TO INCREASE IMMIGRATION IN TAKE: MINISTER
The Federal Immigration Minister has told an urban development conference in Melbourne that there's no need for a significant increase in Australia's immigration intake.
Phillip Ruddock says it's questionable whether Australia could afford some of the short term costs involved in the expansion above current levels.
The Minister predicts Australia's population will eventually stabilise at around 23 million in 25 to 30 years time.
He says that figure's not a government target, but a likely outcome of a declining birth rate combined with the maintenance of the current immigration levels of around 60-thousand a year.
